title: We Don’t Need More Thought Leaders, We Need More Thought Doers
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Joel Salinas argues that the digital world has confused performing insight with practicing wisdom, producing professional opinionists whose main product is more thought leadership. He contends that identity built on sounding smart makes it dangerous to be wrong, and that credibility actually comes from messy, honest execution. Using Proverbs on wisdom as the application of knowledge, he calls for thought doers who test ideas in the field, admit when theories fail and let humility lead. He closes with five practical suggestions, from starting with service to staying human. It is a short character-and-credibility piece aimed at leaders and writers.
points: Leadership credibility comes from doing and admitting failure, not from polished content; identity built on sounding smart makes being wrong dangerous.
Wisdom is knowledge applied, so leaders should test ideas in the field before preaching them.
Execution is vulnerable and slow, and that exposure is the source of trust.
Practical shift: start with service rather than strategy, share the messy middle and let your platform follow your practice.
quotes: Somewhere along the way, we confused the performance of insight with the practice of wisdom. We started celebrating those who talk about solving problems instead of those actually out there doing the work.
It’s not in itself bad, but it can become a trap: when your identity is built around sounding smart, it’s dangerous to be wrong. At that point, you are relying on others acting on your words.
Testing ideas in the field before posting about them. Admitting when a theory doesn’t hold up in reality. Prioritizing experimentation over image. Overall, they let humility lead.

Execution is vulnerable. It's slow. It’s not always glamorous. Sometimes your bold hypothesis turns out to be... just wrong. But that’s where credibility comes from, not in being infallible, but in being honest.

It’s not that knowledge is unimportant; it’s just step 1. But wisdom, defined as the application of knowledge, is what actually leads to transformation. It’s the difference between knowing the right path and walking it.

We don’t need more perfectly posed experts shouting into the digital void. We need more people rolling up their sleeves, doing the work, and then — maybe — turning that into wisdom worth sharing. Because the world doesn’t need another leader with all the right words. It needs leaders who live them.
